name: Merge intervals
brief:
Each interval is a closed pair `{start, end}`. Write `merge_intervals(intervals)`, which joins every group of overlapping or touching intervals and returns the result sorted by start.

The input and the answer are both a `std::vector<std::vector<int>>`.
constraints: The input may be empty and may not be sorted.
Intervals that share an end point merge: [1, 4] and [4, 5] give [1, 5].
Whole numbers up to 2,147,483,647 appear, so never compute `end + 1`.
hint: Sort by start, then keep the last interval of the answer. If the next one starts at or before its end, raise that end to the larger of the two. Otherwise append the next one.

examples.name: Touching ends merge
examples.why: Closed intervals that share an end point are one interval.
examples.note: The two intervals share the point 4.

tests.name: Touching ends merge
tests.why: Closed intervals that share an end point are one interval.
tests.note: The two intervals share the point 4.

tests.name: Unsorted input
tests.why: Sort by start before you sweep. The input is not in order.

tests.name: One inside another
tests.why: The end of the merged interval is the larger of the two ends, not the last one seen.

tests.name: Negative values
tests.why: 2 and 3 are different whole numbers, so [-5, 2] and [3, 4] stay apart.

tests.name: Values at the int limit
tests.why: Compare ends directly. Computing `end + 1` overflows an `int` here.

how: Nine hidden tests call `merge_intervals` with a nested `std::vector<int>` argument and compare the returned nested vector exactly.
notes: Sorting a vector of vectors orders by the first element, then the second.
The test `cur[0] <= out.back()[1]` is what makes touching intervals merge.
